POINTS OF DETERMINATION 15.
The charge framed against the accused is under section 279/338 IPC.

Section 279:- Whoever drives any vehicle, or rides, on any public way in a manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life, or to be likely to cause hurt or injury to any other person, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.

Section 338:- Whoever causes grievous hurt to any person by doing any act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life, or the personal safety of others, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, or with both.

The settled law 16.
The settled principles of law is that in order to invite the wrath of law u/s 279 IPC, the act complained of needs to be either rash or negligent act.

As per Black Law's Dictionary 'negligence' is failure to exercise the standard of care that a reasonably prudent person would have exercised in a similar situation, any conduct that falls below the legal standard established to protect others against an unreasonable risk of harm, except for conduct that is intentionally, wantonly, or wilfully disregardful of others right.
A rash act is primarily an overhasty act and is thus opposed to deliberate act.
In rashness, the criminality lies in running the risk of doing an act with recklessness or indifference to consequences.

25. Hence, as already discussed, it is clear that the evidence of a hostile witness cannot be discarded as a whole and relevant parts thereof which are admissible in law, can be used by the prosecution or the defence, however, it can be subjected to close scrutiny.

26. Driving a heavy vehicle like a cluster bus at speed, in a zig-zag manner, and hitting a two-wheeler from behind clearly constitutes rash and negligent driving, endangering human life, as contemplated under section 279 IPC.
The direct consequence of this act was grievous hurt to PW- 1.

The act falls squarely within the ambit of Section 338 IPC with respect to the grievous hurt caused to PW-1.
27.

The above mentioned circumstances can together be considered as sufficient to hold that accused while driving the offending vehicle with carelessness and had no regard to the possible outcome of his way of driving even when approaching a cautious area on the road.

The MLC of victim/complainant clearly shows injuries to his right leg and as deposed by PW4, it shows deep wound of 134 cm on the right foot with tendon muscle and bone exposed and bruise of 53 cm in right forearm lateral aspect.
The opinion given on MLC is "blunt".
PW1 himself and eye witness PW2 has also deposed that the offending vehicle had run over the right leg of the complainant.

PW4 upon cross examination has admitted that the the original MLC bearing no:
6495/16 placed on judicial record is torn, however, added that she can identify the complete MLC No: from photocopy provided to her by Medical Records department of the hospital.
Moreover, the name and other details on the MLC are also that of the complainant.
Merely because the last digit of the MLC no is torn doesn't mean that the whole testimony of PW4 and the exhibits on the record be discarded.
The MLCs were also proved and there is no reason forthcoming to believe that the MLCs prepared by the attending doctor were false.

Though PW5 has upon cross examination deposed that such injury can also be caused by fall, however, the accused has not been able to highlight any injury which ought to be explained or which could not have been caused due to the accident as alleged.
The defence suggestion that PW-1's motorcycle slipped on garbage or that injuries could be from a fall is not substantiated.

Even if it is assumed that there was a traffic red light signal at the spot, it will only impute more responsibility on the accused to practice caution.
